sections.overview: Acheta domesticus, the house cricket, is a small orthopteran best known from warm human buildings and commercial rearing. Although widely farmed as food for captive animals and people, it is an animal species with its own naturalized populations and a broader ecology than its role as feeder insect suggests.
sections.identification: Adults measure about 13–20 mm in body length in males and 14–20 mm in females; the female’s straight ovipositor adds a further 9–14 mm. They have the typical cricket form, with a laterally compressed body, long antennae, enlarged hind legs for jumping and usually pale yellow-brown coloring with darker markings. The male’s chirp is produced by rubbing the forewings together; nymphs resemble smaller, wingless adults. The cited field descriptions give body length but no standardized adult mass, so no weight is inferred.
sections.habitat: The species is strongly associated with warm places around people, including buildings, food stores and animal-rearing facilities; it can also persist outdoors in sufficiently mild conditions. British records classify it as introduced but widely distributed. Its present range reflects human movement and commerce as well as its original range, which is usually considered to lie in southwestern Asia.
sections.diet: House crickets are omnivorous scavengers. They consume a broad range of plant material and other organic foods, and in captivity accept mixed feeds. A laboratory study found survival differed between mixed, plant-only and animal-only diets, underscoring that diet affects performance; farm rations should not be mistaken for an exact description of wild feeding.
sections.behavior: Males call by stridulation, especially in warm conditions, and the sound can attract females. The species is active in dark, sheltered places and can gather around reliable food and warmth. In dense captive groups, mating and crowding can influence survival, so laboratory longevity values should not be generalized to every wild or farmed cricket.
sections.reproduction: Females place eggs into a suitable moist substrate using the ovipositor. Nymphs hatch and pass through several molts before adulthood. The timing of development depends strongly on temperature and food; one recent review gives a 30–50-day production cycle under rearing conditions, not a universal life-cycle duration in nature.
sections.ecology: As an omnivore, the house cricket consumes plant and animal-derived organic matter and is itself prey for many animals. In places where it has been introduced, it is also closely tied to human food systems and animal feed. The sources used here do not quantify its effects on native communities or identify a single dominant ecological role across its global range.
sections.conservation: The Natural History Museum’s UK species record classifies the cricket as introduced and widely distributed in Britain. No global IUCN assessment or species-wide population trend was verified for this profile; the abundance of farmed crickets does not by itself measure the status of wild populations.
